title: The Holy Land
hook: walking where Jesus walked, and praying for its people

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seven churches of Rome, and Philip Neri's crowd singing between them with lunch in a garden. Your line was pilgrims with a picnic. Did you share a meal with anyone on the way? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-six.

A pilgrim kneels in a low cave under a church in Bethlehem and touches a silver star set into the floor. A few days later she stands on the shore of the Sea of Galilee at dawn. Fishing boats. Gulls. The same water the Gospels keep returning to. Then Jerusalem: narrow stone streets, a shopkeeper calling out, a bell, a call to prayer, a family hurrying to a doorway. She has read these place names her whole life. Nazareth. Capernaum. Gethsemane. Now they're under her feet, and they have weather, and traffic, and neighbors. Some pilgrims come home saying they read the Gospels differently afterward. Today, the land itself.
screen: `A SILVER STAR IN BETHLEHEM.` → `DAWN ON THE SEA OF GALILEE.` → `PLACE NAMES UNDER HER FEET.`

segments.voice: For Christians, what makes this land holy goes back to a line in John's Gospel. It says, in the Douay-Rheims, "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Flesh means a body, and a body stands somewhere. Jesus was born in a particular town, grew up in another, fished and taught by a particular lake, and died outside a particular city wall. First, the phrase in today's line. Some people call the land itself the fifth gospel. The four Gospels are written down. The fifth, they say, is the ground: the hills, the distances, the water. Walking from the lake up into the hills, a pilgrim can feel how far Jesus walked, and why his stories are full of fishermen, sheep and seeds. Second, the shrines. Churches stand over the places tradition links to the Gospel story: the grotto of the Nativity in Bethlehem, the Annunciation in Nazareth, and in Jerusalem the Church of the Holy Sepulchre over the place of the crucifixion and the tomb. Franciscan friars care for many of these shrines on behalf of Catholics. Third, the people. The Holy Land is not a museum. Christian families live there, some in towns their families have called home for generations. Jews and Muslims hold places in the same land holy too, and live there, and pray there. The second half of today's hook matters as much as the first. Catholic pilgrims are encouraged to pray for everyone who lives there, and for peace. Last, the living stones. Pilgrims sometimes say the shrines are the old stones, and the local Christians are the living ones. Both are part of the visit.
screen: `THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH.` · `THE GROUND AS A FIFTH GOSPEL.` · `CHURCHES OVER THE STORY'S PLACES.` · `NOT A MUSEUM: PEOPLE LIVE THERE.` · then, large: `AND DWELT AMONG US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for everyone who lives there. Settle, and breathe. Picture one street in Jerusalem or Bethlehem in the morning. A Christian grandmother opening her shutters. A Jewish father walking his children to school. A Muslim shopkeeper sweeping his step. Children everywhere. Don't sort them. Hold all of them together for a minute: their safety, their work, their sleep tonight. If you pray, you can say, Lord, have mercy, once for each. If you don't, simply wish them peace, one by one. The bell holds the time.
The Holy Land. The places where Jesus was born, lived, died and rose, visited by pilgrims as a kind of fifth gospel, and home to people of more than one faith. Today's word.

Your line: the fifth gospel. Today, read one Gospel scene and look up where it happened on a map. Then pray, or wish peace, for the people who live there now. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics make pilgrimages to the Holy Land, often in parish groups led by a priest, celebrating Mass at shrines such as Bethlehem, Nazareth and the Holy Sepulchre; the Church also asks Catholics to pray and give for the Christians who live there and for peace in the region.

fork.setup: you're on pilgrimage in Bethlehem. your group has an hour free. what do you do with it?

fork.reveal: any of these is fine, but pilgrims are encouraged to meet the living stones: the Christians who live in the land now.

original.note: Greek of John 1:14: the Word became flesh, the line that makes the land holy for Christians.

trapdoor: what you thought: a historic region full of old churches.
what it means: the places where Jesus lived, visited as prayer, and home today to Christians, Jews and Muslims.
what a scholar hears: John 1:14, the Word made flesh: the Incarnation ties the faith to real places, which is why the land is called a fifth gospel.

notes: 'The fifth gospel' is presented as a name 'some people' give the land; it is often attributed to Saint Jerome or to Ernest Renan. Attribution omitted deliberately; confirm.
'Franciscan friars care for many of these shrines on behalf of Catholics': the Custody of the Holy Land; confirm phrasing.
Practice holds Christians, Jews and Muslims together without taking political sides. Confirm the tone is acceptable.
'Lord, have mercy' offered as an existing prayer (the Kyrie), not a new one.
'Living stones' alludes to 1 Peter 2:5, paraphrased; the pilgrim saying is presented as what 'pilgrims sometimes say'.
Fork 'answer' marks meeting local Christians; the reveal says any option is fine. Confirm acceptable for an ungraded fork.
Douay-Rheims wording of John 1:14; Greek original and pronunciation: confirm.

Editor: 'Christians call it the Holy Land because of one line at the center of their faith' (a single-cause and centrality claim) softened to 'for Christians, what makes this land holy goes back to a line in John's Gospel'; local Christian families now 'some' with roots of generations.
